1:
Ellicott opens with an account of how the chapter came to exist. The history of Abram is a succession of brief narratives, possibly written by the patriarch himself; papyrus was known at Ur, but the want of writing material obliged men to short inscriptions like the clay tablets brought thence, some older than Abram. A later narrator would alter such documents very little, which accounts for the recapitulation here; the plain additions, such as the note that one valley was later called the King’s Dale, are credited to Ezra and his men. Gill fixes the moment by the ages, seventy-five and eighty-five, with ten years in Canaan behind them.

Where Hagar came from is contested on her name. Clarke derives it from a Hebrew word for a stranger, and reports a Greek father’s conjecture that she was one of the slaves Pharaoh had given Abram in Egypt. Ellicott derives it from an Arabic verb meaning to flee, concludes it cannot have been her original name, and makes her an Egyptian who had escaped to Abram in the south country and been called, in effect, the run-away.

The idiom for what Sarai hoped to gain is opened by two. Ellicott traces the Hebrew for son, daughter, house and to build to one root, the thought being that children build the house and give a man his pledge of continuance — the tent was the habitation, the house the family — so the phrase is properly that I may be builded by her. Calvin has the same root, and adds the legal point: Sarai claims the child by right of dominion, since handmaids do not bear for themselves. Clarke gives the social rule behind it, that female slaves formed part of a wife’s own patrimony and were hers to dispose of without the husband’s authority, so the slave’s children counted as the mistress’s.

Calvin and Ellicott both work to keep the act from looking merely squalid, and both stop short of excusing it. Calvin refuses to believe so pious a matron ignorant of the promises made to her husband, and argues that a woman wanting a child in the ordinary way would sooner adopt a son than admit a rival, since we know the vehemence of female jealousy; her desire proceeded from the zeal of faith — but not being subjected to God so as to wait his time, she had recourse at once to polygamy, which is nothing but the corruption of lawful marriage. Ellicott notes that monogamy was the original law and the rule in the households of Noah, Terah and Isaac, and that where the narrator first records polygamy he couples it with violence and licence; but he pleads that conduct is influenced by the views of those among whom a man lives, and that Abram, with everything depending on offspring, had taken no step of his own toward another wife but remained content with the barren Sarai.

Henry and Wesley put the blame where the narrative does. Both say that though some excuse may be made for Abram he cannot be justified, since from the beginning it was not so, Christ having reduced the matter to the first institution. Henry observes that the maker of this match was Sarai herself, and draws from it that it is Satan’s policy to tempt us through our nearest relations, the temptation being most dangerous from a hand least suspected, so that our wisdom is to consider not so much who speaks as what is spoken; and God’s commands consult our comfort better than our own contrivances do. Calvin reaches the same warning independently, that Satan sometimes assails us privately through good and simple men, to overcome us unawares. Keil and Delitzsch record the outcome: the scheme reaped nothing but grief and seemed to lose them the maid, until the covenant God turned the whole into a blessing.
3:
Calvin will not let the arrangement be called a marriage and will not call it fornication either. Sarai, he says, did not intend to make her house a brothel, nor to betray her maid’s chastity, nor to act as pander for her husband; yet Hagar is improperly called a wife, having been brought into another person’s bed against the law of God, so that the connection was illicit in this degree, that it stood somewhere between fornication and marriage. He then generalises: the same holds of every invention appended to the word of God, for with whatever fair pretext they are covered there is an inherent corruption in them which degenerates from the purity of the word and vitiates the whole.

Ellicott states the arrangement precisely, and the precision is what makes the quarrel intelligible. Hagar was to be not a concubine but a wife, standing as Sarai’s representative and holding the highest place in the household after her, while remaining Sarai’s maid; the moment she conceived she wished to overthrow that settlement and behaved as though she were Abram’s wife absolutely, thrusting Sarai aside. Clarke, characteristically, reaches for a modern parallel, reporting instances of Hindu women who consent, when barren, to a second marriage for the sake of children, and adding that such marriages often occur without consent. Gill notes only that the two characters are drawn in deliberate contrast, so that the affair might be the more remarkable.

What Hagar did with her advantage draws the sharpest moralising in the chapter. Henry observes that mean and servile spirits, when advanced by God or man, are apt to grow haughty and to forget their origin, since it is a hard thing to bear honour aright; and he adds the harder rule, that we justly suffer by those whom we have sinfully indulged, God making the instruments of our sin the instruments of our trouble — this stone will return upon him that rolleth it. Calvin sees ingratitude, a woman treated with singular kindness beginning to despise her mistress, and bids the faithful accustom themselves to bearing such returns for their kindnesses; but he takes Sarai’s inability to bear it as the more instructive failure.

On Sarai’s charge against her husband the readings differ. Ellicott takes it simply: her act had been one of self-denial for Abram’s sake, and now that it has brought her insolence she holds him answerable. Clarke hears an insinuation in it, that her childlessness was his fault and that he was now more affectionate toward Hagar than toward her; and he reads Abram’s surrender of Hagar as the removal of that suspicion, since he gives back the authority over her that Sarai had conferred. Calvin will allow her nothing: she adduces nothing for which Abram was to be blamed, complains of a contempt she has not asked whether he countenanced, and shows how blind the assault of anger is, rushing impetuously about and condemning those entirely free from blame.

The appeal to God is read by two of them as a danger to the woman who makes it. Calvin points out what she has actually asked for: if God had interposed as judge he must have executed punishment on one or the other, and since Abram had done no injury, the vengeance she imprecated must have fallen on herself. He adds that if ever a woman was of a meek and gentle spirit Sarai excelled in it, so that seeing her patience violently shaken by a single offence should make every one of us the more resolved to govern his own passions. Wesley reaches the same conclusion in three sentences: when passion is upon the throne reason is out of doors and is neither heard nor spoken; those are not always in the right who are most forward in appealing to God; and rash, bold imprecations are commonly evidence of guilt and a bad cause.
6:
Abram’s answer is admired and then examined. Calvin praises its humanity: he does not quarrel with his wife, and though he has the best cause he does not defend it, but voluntarily gives up the wife who had been given him, doing violence to his feelings as husband and father. Wesley draws the domestic rule, that those who would keep peace must answer hard accusations gently, and that husbands and wives should not be both angry at once. But Calvin then puts the harder question: Hagar is with child, and Abram hopes the promised seed is to come from her — why does he not set Sarai aside and turn his care to Hagar? The answer is general: all human contrivances vanish in smoke as soon as a grievous temptation comes, for having taken a wife against the divine command he thought the matter succeeding well while she was pregnant, and at the first contention was at his wit’s end.

Sarai’s treatment is judged by the verb. Clarke says the word implies stripes and hard usage, meant to bring down the body and humble the mind, and adds that if the slave was to blame the mistress is not less liable, since she alone had put Hagar where it was natural to value herself above her mistress. Ellicott renders it more exactly as humbled, that is, reduced to her original condition, and divides the case: it was right that Abram should make her yield due respect, having abused her elevation, but in making her resume her old place as a slave Sarai was possibly unkind. He then adds the observation that ties the chapter together — in running away Hagar showed the untamable love of freedom Ishmael inherited from her, and was repeating the very act from which she had her name.

Henry and Wesley both notice that this is the first appearance of an angel in Scripture, and read the meeting alike. Hagar was making for her own country, her road lying toward Egypt; it were well if our afflictions made us think of our home, the better country; but she was out of the way of her duty and going further astray when the angel found her, and it is a great mercy to be stopped in a sinful way, by conscience or by providence. Henry adds that God suffers wanderers to go on a while, that seeing their folly they may be readier to return.

Who the angel was is argued at length by two and left open by the others. Clarke gives five proofs that the speaker was more than a created being: he promises what God alone can do and foretells what God alone can know; Hagar addresses him as God in the way of worship, which a created angel would have refused; the narrator calls him plainly by the divine name, given to no creature; and he is the same called elsewhere the redeeming Angel and the Angel of the covenant. Gill argues the same, and sets against it the Jewish readings he rejects — that the angel was a prophet of that time, that he was Shem the son of Noah, or that he was a mere man.

Calvin declines the identification and takes a different point: the Lord acts with clemency toward his own though they have deserved punishment, and having mitigated the punishment of Abram and Sarai he casts a paternal look on Hagar, so that his favour extends to the whole family — not sparing them altogether, lest he cherish their vices, but correcting with gentle remedies. He adds that though the form of the vision is not described, he does not doubt it was clothed in a human body in which tokens of celestial glory were conspicuous. Ellicott confines himself to the road, the usual route from Hebron past Beersheba into Egypt, and to the desert of Shur.
8:
The form of address is read the same way by everyone. Gill, Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott all take Hagar, Sarai’s maid as a deliberate check: it tells her she is known, reminds her she is another’s property, and rebukes the flight, since Sarai’s maid ought to be in Sarai’s tent. Ellicott adds the point the others miss, that in bestowing her on Abram Sarai had not ceased to be her mistress. He also notices something about the questions: in these divine communications God’s knowledge of the circumstances is not presumed, but the person visited is led on to tell them, which adds much to the freshness of the narrative. Wesley reads the second question as a warning about where she was going — if she returns to that people she will return to their gods.

Ellicott then overturns the reading of the previous verse. The word rendered submit thyself is the very word rendered dealt hardly a few lines earlier: the angel commands her to take the position Sarai was forcing on her, which proves there had been no personal maltreatment at all — commentators, he says, have taken that notion not from the Hebrew but from the English version. Clarke, who had taken the word to imply stripes and hard usage, is thereby answered from within the chapter.

Calvin uses the command for a long defence of subjection that is worth reading with its date in mind. The epithet declares that Hagar remained a servant though she had escaped her mistress, since liberty is not obtained by stealth or flight but by manumission; God thereby shows he approves of civil government and that violating it is inexcusable. He grants that servitude was then hard and gives thanks that the barbarity has been abolished, yet holds that God declared from heaven that servants should bear the yoke, and that the apostle does not free them but only commands they be kindly treated. He then extends it: if masters deal too hardly with servants, or rulers treat their subjects with unjust asperity, the rigour is still to be endured, and there is no just cause for shaking off the yoke.

Ellicott states the exchange as a bargain, and it is the clearest account of the chapter’s logic. The purpose of the appearance is that Abram’s son should not be lost among the population of Egypt but become the father of a free people; Hagar will therefore submit to her lot as a slave to secure liberty for her offspring. Henry frames it as encouragement, that God meets with mercy those returning to their duty, and finds comfort in the notice taken of her condition, since it is a great comfort to women with child to think they are under the particular care of providence.

That an angel should promise what only God can perform is faced by three. Clarke asks the question outright and answers that the speaker plainly uses the authority proper to God. Gill takes the speaker to be the Lord himself, and reports without approving the rabbinic notion that a fresh angel was sent at each speech, some counting four and some five, without any reason. Calvin allows that God commonly invests his ministers with his own character so their word may carry the greater authority, but does not disapprove the ancient opinion that Christ the Mediator was present in all the oracles. He adds a fine remark on the method: God might have enjoined what was right by bare authority, but allures her to obedience, mingling mild and paternal invitations with his commands, since he will not draw us by servile methods. Wesley notes the doubled Hebrew verb, multiplying I will multiply, and supposes the Turks of his own day to be Ishmael’s descendants. Keil and Delitzsch simply carry the speeches through to Hagar’s naming of the God who sees.
11:
That Hagar had not prayed is noticed by three, each differently. Calvin observes that we do not read of her having recourse to prayer, and are left to conjecture that when she was stupefied by her sufferings the angel came of his own accord; from which he distinguishes two ways in which God helps men, when they implore his aid as suppliants, and when, unasked, he succours them. Clarke says afflictions have a voice in the ears of God even when prayer is restrained. Wesley puts it shortest: even where there is little cry of devotion, the God of pity hears the cry of affliction, for tears speak as well as prayers.

The name is read as a memorial rather than a character. Clarke says it must keep the mother in remembrance of God’s interposition and remind the child that he was an object of providential goodness. Ellicott notes that, like Samuel, Ishmael received his name from the events of his mother’s life and not from anything in his own, adding that Genesis follows no rule in naming children. Calvin observes the oddity that an honourable name is granted to one he takes for a reprobate, and explains it as a monument of the kindness with which God embraced the whole house of Abram: the covenant of eternal life did not belong to Ishmael, yet God would not leave him wholly without favour.

The phrase rendered a wild man is literally a wild-ass man, and the animal divides them. Ellicott insists the wild ass of the Arabian deserts is a very noble creature, chosen in Job to exemplify the greatness of God, its marks being great speed, love of solitude and an untamable fondness for liberty — the exact type of the Bedouin who despises the ease of a settled life. Clarke quotes the same passage of Job at length as the best description of the Ishmaelites, and draws the political conclusion: God himself has sent them out free and loosed them from all political restraint. Gill turns it into history, that neither Assyrian, Mede, Persian, Greek nor Roman subdued them, and that the Arabs of his own day oblige the Turks to pay yearly for the passage of pilgrims to Mecca.

Calvin will not have the wild ass at all. He rejects the reading that makes Ishmael a forester, and says the simple meaning is a warlike man, so formidable that none shall injure him with impunity; the context, not etymology, must settle it. He then asks the question the others avoid: is it to be reckoned among God’s benefits that a man should keep his place by force of arms, when nothing is more desirable than peace? His answer grades the blessings. Peace with all men is among the chief; it is here denied to Ishmael, so the blessing next in order is granted instead, that he shall not be overcome but shall be brave enough to resist. No unmixed blessing is promised, only a tolerable condition — and it is by no means to be counted a benefit that he should have enemies on every side.

Wesley divides the verse and gives its halves different offices: his hand against every man is his sin, every man’s hand against him is his punishment; those of turbulent spirit commonly have troublesome lives, and the injurious must expect repayment in their own coin. On the last clause he takes the sense to be that though threatened by all his neighbours Ishmael will keep his ground, for Abram’s sake more than his own. Ellicott gives it the same sense, that he shall maintain his independence among the other Abrahamic nations, but reports that many prefer to render it that he shall dwell to the east of his brethren, which is certainly the meaning in one later passage though it suits another less well.
13:
Hagar’s name for God is read three ways. Ellicott insists it does not mean a God who sees all things, as one Aramaic version paraphrases, but a God who permits himself to be seen; and he takes her following words as her own explanation, a play on the word meaning, do I not see, and therefore am alive, not even blinded, though I have seen God. Clarke reports that sense too — her surprise at surviving a sight of God, since any who saw him were supposed to be consumed — but proposes another, since the word rendered after elsewhere means the latter times: have I here also seen the latter purposes of him that seeth me, referring her words to what had just been told her of her descendants.

Calvin declines both and calls the God of vision reading forced. What Hagar has come to see, he says, is that she who thought herself carried through the desert by chance now perceives that human affairs are under divine government — and whoever is persuaded that God looks upon him must walk as in his sight. The editorial matter printed with him again dissents in his own margin, noting that the interpretation he calls forced has the sanction of the highest literary authorities, listing seven. Gill reports the three Targums, which make her pray, or give thanks, or both, and observes that the ancient synagogue took the angel for the Word of the Lord.

Calvin makes the naming of the well the measure of her change. He takes the name to have originated with her, not content with one confession but wishing God’s mercy attested in time to come, so that she transmitted her testimony as from hand to hand; and he infers how useful it is that those who will not freely humble themselves should be subdued by stripes, since Hagar, always wild and having shaken off the yoke, now appears altogether another person. But he adds the qualification that saves the remark: she was not reduced to order by stripes only, a celestial vision being added, and the same is necessary for us, that God while chastising us should also bring us to meekness by his Spirit.

The name of the well is turned to different account by each. Gill allows it to mean either the well of him that liveth and seeth me or the well of her that liveth and seeth, and reports a Jewish commentator identifying it with a well near Mecca which the Arabs call Hagar’s. Clarke finds two things implied, a dedication of the well to him who appeared there, and faith in the promise, since the Living One who exists in all generations can accomplish what is fulfilled through the whole lapse of time. Wesley draws the lesson, that those admitted to communion with God should tell others what he has done for their souls.

Clarke closes by defending Abram and Henry by using him as a type. Clarke asks why he is blamed at all: God had not yet told him how the heir was to come, and concubinage under that dispensation was perfectly lawful — adding, from another writer, that Ishmael is the first man named by God before his birth. Henry takes the birth as the fruit of obedience, that those who obey divine precepts shall have the comfort of divine promises, and then reads it through the apostle: this was the son of the bondwoman born after the flesh, and many who can call Abraham father are born after the flesh, the carnal seed in the church being sooner brought forth than the spiritual, since it is easier to persuade men to assume the form of godliness than to submit to its power. Keil and Delitzsch add that Abram probably regarded this child as the promised seed until, thirteen years later, God’s counsel was more clearly unfolded.
